extracted.intended_audience: machine learning researchers, conference organizers, and peer reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: An analytic essay identifying ethical problems and quality risks in the peer-review process used by large machine-learning conferences and proposing possible mitigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: De facto review process features
rubrics_metrics.description: The review process in large-scale ML conferences is a double-blind process that includes one rebuttal period; it typically lasts ~9–10 weeks followed by a 1-week rebuttal. Reviewers choose papers via a bidding system or by invitation of an Area Chair (AC). Each paper is reviewed by on average 3–4 reviewers supervised by an AC. Each reviewer provides a numerical score and a confidence score. Depending on the conference, authors may reply to single reviewers (e.g., on OpenReview) or reply to all reviewers in one PDF page (e.g., NeurIPS). Roughly 2–3 weeks after rebuttal the AC issues the final decision based on a posteriori rebuttal reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the baseline/procedural standard against which problems are evaluated; variations between conferences (OpenReview vs NeurIPS) and timing (rebuttal length, decision latency) are noted as relevant. Understanding these procedural elements is necessary when proposing fixes (e.g., randomization, multiple blind groups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment of reviewers and lack of reviewing experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Conferences rely on the community (unpaid reviewers) to scale reviewing capacity; increasing submissions require proportionally more reviewers, but the pool of qualified reviewers grows more slowly. Conferences have lightened reviewer eligibility, leading to many junior (PhD or even master) students being recruited as reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem effects: increased likelihood of poor-quality reviews and a sense of randomness in decisions. Examples: NeurIPS 2016 used author-nominated reviewers (36% recruited this way) resulting in many junior reviewers; ICML 2020 had self-nominated reviewers. Proposed remedies include introducing mandatory coursework on reviewing in curricula, mentorship programs for novice reviewers, reviewer training/mentorship (workshop evidence from NeurIPS 2020), and limiting the number of papers assigned per reviewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringements of the double-blind process
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors publishing preprints (e.g., arXiv) or releasing code (e.g., GitHub) can break double-blindness and induce bias in reviews. Empirical evidence shows a positive correlation between acceptance rate and papers with high-reputation preprints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: de-anonymization may cause less-confident reviewers to favor well-known authors. Proposed mitigations: allow anonymous preprints (anonymized arXiv-style posting) or, more extremely, forbid preprints during review. Trade-offs are acknowledged: banning preprints reduces dissemination velocity and has costs for the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent behavior in bidding systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Bidding systems permit reviewers to choose which papers to review, which can lead to quid-pro-quo arrangements, collusion, deliberate negative reviewing (torpedo reviewing), and rational cheating (rejecting competitors' work). Such strategic behavior reduces fairness and can harm research directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and harms: documented collusion cases in ACM/IEEE communities; the risk of a few reviewers killing new research directions; tragic anecdotes cited. Proposed solutions: randomization of reviewer assignments (to reduce ability to target papers), and algorithmic approaches to mitigate manipulation (referenced works proposing randomized assignment algorithms). Trade-offs: randomization may reduce matching quality and thus review quality unless mitigations are designed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biases in numerical ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Mapping subjective opinions to a single numerical rating is difficult; selection bias causes average ratings to be positively skewed (users/reviewers select already top-ranked items to rate). Conformity bias during the rebuttal/discussion phase can lead less-confident reviewers to conform to more confident reviewers' opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: distorted numeric scores that do not reflect objective quality. Proposed mitigations: replace or complement numerical ratings with comparisons or rankings; use multiple independent groups of reviewers blind to each other who review the same paper and randomize reviews; base AC decisions on randomized/blinded aggregations to reduce conformity. References point to research on rating difficulty, selection bias, and conformity effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: The appendix (supplementary material) phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: A growing portion of essential results is placed in appendices/supplementary material. This 'appendix phenomenon' arises from an arms race for comprehensiveness and leads reviewers to request yet more work; moreover, many reviewers do not read supplementary material, so important results go unreviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: threat to proper validation and dissemination of scientific knowledge. Proposed remedies: limit the number of pages per submission or explicitly limit appendix/supplementary pages; require authors to state results within a limited page count or encourage submission to journals if more space is needed; consider removing the possibility of uploading supplementary material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested countermeasures (aggregated mitigations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper lists several concrete measures to address the identified problems: (1) introduce appropriate training/mentorship for new scholars; (2) randomize the review process; (3) anonymize preprints; (4) use rankings instead of numerical ratings; (5) have multiple groups of reviewers blind to each other; (6) limit or remove supplementary material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as potential remedies; the paper notes trade-offs and that each issue deserves more space. Some mitigations are cross-cutting (e.g., randomization addresses bidding fraud and reviewer selection bias) while others trade off against community norms (e.g., anonymizing or banning preprints reduces dissemination speed). References to algorithmic proposals and experiments are given for several measures.
